extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, fiction writers, and literary critics studying craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and balancing dramatic (scene/action) and pictorial (description/background) methods in novel-writing — when to let characters enact the story, when to supply authorial survey, and how to use setting to support drama. Includes examples and anti-patterns (Balzac, Dickens, Henry James, Stevenson) illustrating economy, credibility, and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the issue unfold within the situation (show, don't comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: To see the issue slowly unfolding and flowering out of the middle of a situation, and to watch it emerge unaided, with everything that it has to say said by the very lines and masses of its structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer allowing the story and characters' actions to reveal meaning rather than relying on an authorial spokesman who 'pours out his information.' The spokesman/narrator who over-explains is often unnecessary and diminishes the immediacy and drama of the scene. Aim for dramatic immediacy where the action itself communicates the important points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrust the story to the people in it (dramatic method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story-tellers should often 'entrust the story to the people in it' and cast dramatic motive into round action when suitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a subject lends itself to action, prefer a dramatic presentation (scenes, dialogue, enacted incidents) that gives direct force and validity. Drama is 'paramount' for placing and establishing a piece of action. However, be aware of limits — drama may be hampered when wider background or atmosphere is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial/authorial survey to supply background and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The seeing eye of the author, which can sweep broadly and generalize the sense of what it sees, will more naturally relate action to its surroundings than strict drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the effect of a story depends on time, place, or the outlying associations of the scene, employ descriptive, pictorial narration to supply breadth, depth, and colour that pure dramatic scenes cannot convey economically. Use broad survey to render the 'background of the action' so it makes full impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance drama and picture according to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama gives validity and direct force; the pictorial impression provides breadth and supporting atmosphere — both have distinct strengths and should be used where each is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work both ways: begin from pictorial summary and proceed to drama, or start with drama and supplement with broad survey. Choose the method that suits the subject: some stories require dramatic immediacy, others require detailed background; many need a mixture. Experiment and justify departures from the 'sound rule.'

rubrics_metrics.name: When setting is singular, render it clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story 'requires and postulates such a very particular background, so singular and so artificial,' the background must be made as effective as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story depends on a small, definite social milieu (example: Nanda in The Awkward Age), the novelist must ensure the setting is 'clearly seen and known.' Failure to establish the quality of civilization or milieu will leave central characters under-rendered. Use description or staged scenes as needed to make setting intelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary authorial exposition (the over-voluble chronicler)
rubrics_metrics.description: The instant authority of drama is neglected by the 'deep-breathed narrator' who strides from volume to volume and pours out information; his constant talk can drown action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the impulse to inform the reader through excessive authorial commentary. If the drama can reveal material, suppress the explanatory spokesman. Use exposition only when drama cannot reasonably supply the necessary information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of drama's limits to express outlying associations
rubrics_metrics.description: The play-form, and fiction purely dramatic in method, is hampered in its power to express the outlying associations of its scene; it is vivid and compact but narrow, with little depth for atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the novel's effect requires relating action to wider social or atmospheric associations, supplement scenic action with broader narration. Pure drama can express background but at greater effort; prefer pictorial methods when economy and ease of conveying atmosphere matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use background description as an engine for action (Balzac model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac 'masses' pictorial impressions and preparatory pictures until, when the action begins, the setting's accumulated force propels the drama forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate, detailed scene-setting can provide character and energy for the subsequent action — e.g., Maison Vauquer in Pere Goriot becomes a fully created impression that gives immediacy and weight to the events. Use preparatory description as a reserve of vigour to drive drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice economy: ensure descriptive detail is functional
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac sometimes indulged in the 'lust of description for its own sake,' but his lengthy research among furniture and facts often ends by creating a scene in which action can move rapidly 'without losing any of its due emphasis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While detail can enrich setting, beware of needless digression into particulars irrelevant to the story's action. Descriptive fullness should serve the drama — if a detail 'is needed' use it; if not, avoid excessive ornament that distracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing irrelevant associations from other works when reusing characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who reappear from other books (Balzac's recurring figures) carry old associations that, if irrelevant to the present story, will 'disturb the unity of the story and confuse its truth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reusing familiar characters across works, in a given story restrict what reappears to what is relevant to that story's foreground action. Excessive back-reference or latent histories from other books can obstruct the reader's view of the protagonist's world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone down incredible or overcharged drama with pictorial qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: If the dramatic method leaves the story 'too much... too searching and too betraying' or likely to seem harsh, overcharged, or romantic, it should be 'restrained, qualified, toned down' by the art of the picture-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descriptive scene or gradual pictorial approbation to make spectacular or romantic action appear plausible and less theatrical. Embedding a marvelous plot in a familiar, well-established world reduces its apparent falsity (examples: Balzac attempting to embed romance in realism; Dickens succeeding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce fantastic or romantic intrigues gradually within a credible scene (Dickens method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dickens 'leads gradually into' romantic intrigues 'through well-populated scenes of character and humour' so that by the time the plot thickens the world 'is actual' and 'compels belief.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a broad, richly populated picture before concentrating on romantic or sensational climax. Prepare the reader with a believable world (characters, humour, daily life) so a later violent or mysterious plot-sequence seems natural rather than jarring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use first-person narration strategically to dramatize or to picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Rendering events as 'somebody's narrative' can be the first step towards dramatization (and can also tone or qualify drama into picture). The same device can have different effects depending on subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose first-person narration when you want to filter drama through a participant's view, either to heighten immediacy or to present the action as a personalized picture; e.g., Esmond (enhances picture), The Master of Ballantrae (tones the drama). Match voice to desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crystallize incidental characters sharply when presenting them dramatically
rubrics_metrics.description: When a broad picture is translated into action (as Dickens does), incidental characters must be 'crystallized and formulated' very sharply — often labelled with a trick or phrase — because their opportunities are strictly limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dramatic presentation of many minor characters, make each instantly recognizable through a strong trait or phrase so they function effectively within the few scenes allotted. This economy avoids diffuse sketches and secures dramatic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve 'tour de force' dramatic minimalism for justified cases
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel that is 'as bare of all background as a play of Racine' or seeks to render general life 'in the particular action, and in the action alone' is a tour de force and should be attempted only when the effect justifies the difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rejecting the novelist's privileges (description) without good cause. Only pursue strict dramatic minimalism when it serves the book's coherence and effect (e.g., Princesse de Cleves) — otherwise use available pictorial resources to support the action.
